verdicts.trueWording: most of these stories mean whatever the text of the story is
verdicts.note: Raw Wayback capture of NYRSF fetched and read. Sentence appears verbatim in the allegory paragraph, opening 'So most of these stories...'. Byline 'A Story' / Kim Stanley Robinson, dated 09/06/2013, NYRSF issue 301 (Sept 2013) - all attribution limbs confirmed on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: catechisms, interrogations, examinations, Socratic dialogues, classroom lessons
verdicts.note: Verbatim in the question-and-answer paragraph; the list continues 'badgering sessions, and many other forms'. The 'set-piece dialogue' limb is supported by the very next sentence, which names 'this tendency for set piece dialogue'.

verdicts.trueWording: pastiches of anthropological reports, fairy tales, aboriginal tales
verdicts.note: Verbatim in the pastiche paragraph. Robinson does not himself sort the list into fiction/non-fiction, but anthropological reports are listed and the same list carries other non-fiction forms (movie reviews, hunting articles), so the claim's 'non-fiction forms' reading holds on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: had a sentimental idea, he chose a sentimental style
verdicts.note: Verbatim, same pastiche paragraph: Robinson reports 'He once told me that since "Our Neighbor, by David Copperfield"' had a sentimental idea, he chose a sentimental style. Reported-speech limb ('Wolfe telling him') confirmed.

verdicts.trueWording: identified as a fiction written by a minor character
verdicts.note: Verbatim in the story-suite paragraph, which opens 'Another suite is made by the three novellas in The Fifth Head of Cerberus'; the clause ends 'in the first story'. Every limb on the page.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'than most fantasies do' - the comment reads 'than a lot of fantasies', a weaker comparison class
verdicts.trueWording: they give more clues to the world around the reader
verdicts.note: Live Lorehaven page fetched with a browser UA; comment thread present in the raw HTML. Matt Mikalatos, reply opening 'Hey Becky', timestamped March 15, 2013 at 11:24 pm (the claim's source line says 16 March - one day off, probably timezone). He writes of 'the obscure language and things'; the quotation is verbatim except that the page's comparison is 'a lot of fantasies', not 'most'.

verdicts.trueWording: By framing the text as translation... language and its reliability
verdicts.note: ultan.org.uk fetched live. Section 'Who Writes?' In the same section Crampton writes of manuscripts Wolfe 'merely "edits" or "translates"' and of two writings 'supposedly translated by Wolfe'. The page's exact formulation is 'pointing to the question of language and its reliability'; the claim compresses this to 'the reliability of language', which is the same move.

verdicts.trueWording: we are warned against possible errors of translation in the preface
verdicts.note: Verbatim in section 'Who Writes?', the clause closing 'to Soldier of the Mist'. Article bylined Jeremy Crampton, dated 10 August 2000, with an afterword saying it was written in the late 1980s (c.1988) - both source limbs confirmed.

verdicts.trueWording: ranging from cleanliness and love of order to courage
verdicts.note: Verbatim under the heading 'Loyalty and "Arete"'. Crampton introduces it as Wolfe's own definition and cites it to (Arete, Glossary); the entry opens 'the virtues of a soldier' and closes on courage in the face of death, so the claimed range is exact.

verdicts.trueWording: one knows what the words mean, that they actually mean it
verdicts.note: Verbatim in section 'Who Writes?'; Crampton's quotation runs on '...and that they cannot ever mean anything else. All of which is seldom true'. Its footnote 9 is Gene Wolfe [untitled] in R. Jackson (ed.), Frontier Crossings, Conspiracy '87, 1987, p.119 - the claim's citation limb confirmed on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: can be read by an educated reader, and reread with increased pleasure
verdicts.note: gwern PDF fetched and text-extracted (6 pages). On printed p.82 (PDF p.4) Gaiman says he has used the line 'ever since I read it in a letter where you defined good literature', then quotes Wolfe's definition verbatim. Letter, quoted-back-by-Gaiman and definition limbs all on the page. Issue confirmed as Locus 500, September 2002 ('This is Issue 500').

verdicts.trueWording: The second novella is a story told by one of the characters
verdicts.note: Printed p.81 (PDF p.3), GW speaking of The Fifth Head of Cerberus after Gaiman's 'Those three stories interweave': 'A lot of readers consider it a sort of three-part novel', then the quoted sentence, ending 'in the third novella, and so on'. Every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: it assures the reader that things need not be as they are
verdicts.note: Printed p.82, both in the body and as the page's pull-quote. Gaiman asks 'What's the most important thing about fiction?'; Wolfe answers with the quoted sentence, ending 'as they are now. In other words, the most important thing is hope.'

verdicts.trueWording: Remember, I was a journalist on an industrial magazine, Plant Engineering
verdicts.note: Printed p.82, GW, continuing 'I've been in a ton of industrial plants' and describing plants 'right out of Dante' and a rubber tire plant. Gaiman's next question, 'To what extent does that stuff wind up in the fiction?', draws 'You can't help drawing upon yourself... transmute them into a coherent story', supporting the grounding limb; the issue's own bio gives the span (Plant Engineering, 1972-84), supporting 'years'.

verdicts.trueWording: It's very tempting to define terms, put your own prejudices in
verdicts.note: Printed p.7 (PDF p.2), GW, in the exchange about dictionaries and guidebooks; the sentence ends 'as Samuel Johnson did' and is preceded by 'Ambrose Bierce was the original guy in that area'. Quotation and both limbs verbatim on the page.
